System design

How to choose the right solar system size

Consumption first, roof second, equipment last — a repeatable method for sizing a solar system, with the arithmetic shown.

Published 3 June 2026Updated 15 October 20268 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

System size is the decision everything else hangs from: what it costs, what it generates, how much you still buy from the grid and how quickly the investment looks sensible. It is also the decision most often made by guesswork. This article sets out a method you can follow — and challenge — using your own numbers.

Step one: establish your annual consumption

Everything begins with how many kilowatt hours your household uses in a year. There are three ways to find out, in increasing order of accuracy:

Three ways to estimate annual consumption
MethodHow it worksConfidence
Annual bill totalAdd four quarterly bills (or one annual statement) in dollars and divide by your average usage rateRough — throws away all timing information
Bill plus rate checkTotal kWh shown on the bills, summed across the yearGood — actual metered totals per quarter
Interval data downloadHalf-hourly usage from your retailer or network portalBest — shows exactly when you use power, which is what sizing actually depends on

The third method is the one worth asking for. A household that uses 6,000 kWh per year with most of it in the evening needs a different design from one with the same total spread through the day — even though both would be sold 'a 6.6 kW system' by a template proposal.

Step two: estimate what a kilowatt produces on your roof

Across Australia, a kilowatt of panels produces broadly between 1,200 and 1,650 kilowatt hours per year, depending on location — sunnier regions and better angles at the top of the range. Shade, roof pitch and direction adjust that upward or downward; as a working method, pick a regional figure, then apply a roof factor (say 0.8 for significant shade, 0.9 for a good but not perfect plane, 1.0 for an ideal one).

Then the arithmetic is simple division. If a household uses 4,800 kWh per year, and their roof is expected to yield 1,400 kWh per kilowatt after shade, the array that generates roughly their consumption is 4,800 ÷ 1,400 ≈ 3.4 kW. Those figures are an illustration of the method, not a prediction for any specific address — the point is to see where every number comes from.

Step three: adjust for when you use power

Generating your annual consumption is a target, not an obligation. The real question is how much of the generation the house can use or store. Three levers move the answer:

  • Daytime presence — a household that is home during the day (working from home, heat pumps, pool, daytime air-conditioning) can self-consume a large share of midday generation.
  • A battery — storage converts otherwise-exported surplus into evening supply, which raises the useful ceiling on array size.
  • Export limits — some networks cap how much you may export, which is another reason generation without a use has a lower value.

Step four: the two failure modes

Undersizing is the more common mistake in quotes: a small template system that produces far less than the household uses, leaving expensive evening imports untouched. It is popular because it prices well in an advertisement.

Oversizing is the more expensive mistake: an array so large that most generation is exported at a fraction of the retail rate. For households without storage and with modest daytime use, every kilowatt beyond what can be self-consumed or usefully stored earns less than the first ones did.

A battery changes the optimal answer

When storage is planned, a somewhat larger array can be justified, because surplus has somewhere to go besides a low feed-in tariff. When no battery is expected, sizing to — or slightly below — consumption usually produces the better return. The savings estimator models both cases side by side.

Rules of thumb, used carefully

Industry shorthand like 'kilowatts equal to three times the daily average use' circulates widely. Such rules are fine as a sanity check on a proposal, and dangerous as the basis for a design: they assume average shade, average tariffs, average household behaviour — and your house is not average in all three. The method in this article takes minutes longer and lands somewhere defensible.

Key takeaways

  • Annual consumption in kilowatt hours is the anchor number — get it from interval data if possible.
  • Regional yield of roughly 1,200–1,650 kWh per kW, adjusted for shade, converts consumption into an array size.
  • Timing of use decides how much generation is actually useful to you.
  • Undersizing wastes potential; oversizing exports cheap and imports dear.
  • Planned storage justifies a somewhat larger array; uncertain storage plans do not.
